title: Need scheduled, parameterized reports (Excel/PDF/CSV) on Azure SQL + Power BI Pro. Where should I spend?
summary: Current setup Azure SQL Database (Standard S2, DTU model). No linked servers or cross-database queries. Power BI Pro for dashboards (40 users, 3 authors). We have no tool for scheduled or paginated reports, and no SQL Server licenses or Fabric capacity. What we need Automated Excel, PDF and delimited-text (CSV/pipe/tab) reports Delivery by email and to a network share drive (SFTP would be a bonus, but we can move files with external processes) Parameterized subscriptions, with a large list of them managed from a table, like SSRS data-driven subscriptions About [N] reports and [N] recipients, mostly monthly Background At past jobs we used SSRS or Crystal Reports, and SSRS would fit. But SQL Server 2025 shipped without it (2022 is the last version), and Power BI Report Server replaces it. We don't own SQL Server, so a license would be a new $8k spend just to host reporting. I can only fund one path. Options I'm weighing Fabric F2 (1-year reserved, about $1.9k/yr), scaling to F4 on report days. Power BI paginated reports plus subscriptions. As I understand it, delivery goes to email and OneDrive/SharePoint, and per-recipient dynamic subscriptions are email only. For file shares and bulk parameterized runs I'd need to build something with Power Automate, Logic Apps or the Export API. SQL Server 2025 license (about $8k) to run Power BI Report Server. On-prem, with data-driven subscriptions and file share delivery. Needs a server to host it. A third-party scheduler (PBRS or similar) on top of Power BI. Questions Has anyone built SSRS-style data-driven subscriptions on Fabric paginated reports plus Power Automate or the Export API? How did it hold up (throttling, timeouts, failures)? Can an F2/F4 handle paginated report exports from an S2 Azure SQL database without throttling? When scaling a reserved F2 up to F4 for a few days each month, how is the extra billed? title: The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly
summary: From roundabouts to the stock market, relentless streamlining could be making the world more dangerous We have all been there: packed shoulder to shoulder on the train while the person beside us coughs and sneezes. A protective flu jab offers some reassurance, but so does the thought that there will be a hospital bed for you, should you need it. Yet, in England, about 95% of adult hospital beds were occupied at the height of flu season last year. If hospitals were hotels, that level of occupancy would be good business, and we would commend them for their efficiency. But do we really want a hospital to have so few beds in reserve that it’s just one bad flu week away from having to treat patients in corridors? Continue reading...
